title: Abstract Algebra II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Abstract Algebra II curriculum, building on MTH300 (introductory group theory): subgroups, cyclic groups, cosets and Lagrange's Theorem, normal subgroups and quotient groups, group homomorphisms and the isomorphism theorems, permutation groups, an introduction to Sylow theory, and an introduction to rings, ideals, integral domains, and fields.

questions.question: A nonempty subset H of a group G is a subgroup of G if:
options: H is closed under the group operation and contains inverses of its elements
H has the same number of elements as G
H is any subset of G
questions.correct_answer: H is closed under the group operation and contains inverses of its elements
questions.explanation: The subgroup criterion requires closure under the operation and closure under taking inverses (and containing the identity, which follows from these).

questions.question: By the subgroup test, a nonempty finite subset H of a group G is a subgroup if and only if:
options: H is closed under the group operation
questions.correct_answer: H is closed under the group operation
questions.explanation: For a nonempty finite subset of a group, closure under the operation alone is sufficient to guarantee it is a subgroup (inverses follow automatically).

questions.question: A cyclic group is one that:
options: can be generated by a single element
questions.correct_answer: can be generated by a single element
questions.explanation: A cyclic group G = ⟨g⟩ consists of all powers (or multiples, additively) of a single generator g.

questions.question: Every cyclic group is necessarily:
questions.correct_answer: abelian
questions.explanation: Since every element is a power of the same generator, elements of a cyclic group always commute, making it abelian.

questions.question: In the cyclic group Z12 (integers mod 12 under addition), the order of the element 4 is:
questions.explanation: The order of 4 is 12/gcd(4,12) = 12/4 = 3, since 4+4+4 = 12 ≡ 0 (mod 12).

questions.question: For a subgroup H of a finite group G, a left coset gH is defined as:
questions.correct_answer: {gh : h ∈ H}
questions.explanation: The left coset of H by g consists of all products gh formed by multiplying g on the left by each element of H.

questions.question: Lagrange's Theorem states that for a finite group G and subgroup H:
options: the order of H divides the order of G
the order of G divides the order of H
questions.correct_answer: the order of H divides the order of G
questions.explanation: Lagrange's Theorem states |H| divides |G|, since G is partitioned into cosets of H, each of size |H|.

questions.question: A direct consequence of Lagrange's Theorem is that a group of prime order p:
options: has no proper nontrivial subgroups and is cyclic
questions.correct_answer: has no proper nontrivial subgroups and is cyclic
questions.explanation: Since the only divisors of a prime p are 1 and p, any nontrivial element generates the whole group, forcing it to be cyclic with no proper nontrivial subgroups.

questions.question: A subgroup N of G is called normal if:
options: gNg^{-1} = N for every g in G
questions.correct_answer: gNg^{-1} = N for every g in G
questions.explanation: A normal subgroup is invariant under conjugation by every element of G, i.e. gNg^{-1} = N for all g ∈ G.

questions.question: In an abelian group, every subgroup is:
questions.correct_answer: normal
questions.explanation: Since gh = hg for all elements in an abelian group, gNg^{-1} = N automatically for every subgroup N.

questions.question: If N is a normal subgroup of G, the quotient group G/N consists of:
options: the set of cosets of N in G, with coset multiplication as the operation
the elements of G not in N
the intersection of G and N
questions.correct_answer: the set of cosets of N in G, with coset multiplication as the operation
questions.explanation: The quotient group G/N is formed from the cosets of N, and normality of N ensures coset multiplication (aN)(bN) = (ab)N is well-defined.

questions.question: The order of the quotient group G/N (for G finite and N normal) is given by:
questions.explanation: The order of the quotient group equals the index of N in G, which is |G| divided by |N|.

questions.question: A function φ: G → H between groups is a homomorphism if:
options: φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b in G
φ maps every element to the identity
questions.correct_answer: φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all a, b in G
questions.explanation: A group homomorphism is a structure-preserving map: it satisfies φ(ab) = φ(a)φ(b) for all elements a, b.

questions.question: The kernel of a group homomorphism φ: G → H is defined as:
questions.correct_answer: {g ∈ G : φ(g) = eH}
questions.explanation: The kernel consists of all elements of G that map to the identity element eH of H under φ.

questions.question: The kernel of any group homomorphism is always:
options: a normal subgroup of the domain
questions.correct_answer: a normal subgroup of the domain
questions.explanation: The kernel of a homomorphism is always a normal subgroup, since for any g ∈ G and k ∈ ker φ, φ(gkg^{-1}) = φ(g)φ(k)φ(g)^{-1} = eH.

questions.question: A homomorphism φ: G → H is injective (one-to-one) if and only if:
questions.correct_answer: ker φ = {e}
questions.explanation: A homomorphism is injective precisely when its kernel contains only the identity element.

questions.question: The First Isomorphism Theorem states that for a homomorphism φ: G → H:
questions.correct_answer: G/ker(φ) ≅ im(φ)
questions.explanation: The First Isomorphism Theorem states the quotient of G by the kernel of φ is isomorphic to the image of φ.

questions.question: Two groups G and H are called isomorphic if there exists:
options: a homomorphism that is not injective
questions.correct_answer: a bijective homomorphism between them
questions.explanation: An isomorphism is a homomorphism that is also a bijection, establishing that G and H have identical algebraic structure.

questions.question: The symmetric group Sn consists of:
options: all cyclic groups of order n
questions.correct_answer: all permutations of n objects
questions.explanation: Sn is the group of all bijections (permutations) of a set of n elements, under composition, with order n!.

questions.question: The order of the symmetric group S4 is:
questions.explanation: The order of Sn is n!; for n=4, |S4| = 4! = 24.

questions.question: A permutation is called even if it can be expressed as:
options: a product of an even number of transpositions
a product of an odd number of transpositions
questions.correct_answer: a product of an even number of transpositions
questions.explanation: Every permutation decomposes into transpositions; the parity (even/odd) of that number is invariant and defines the sign of the permutation.

questions.question: The set of even permutations in Sn forms a subgroup called:
questions.correct_answer: the alternating group An
questions.explanation: The alternating group An is precisely the subgroup of Sn consisting of all even permutations, and it has order n!/2.

questions.question: In cycle notation, the permutation (1 2 3) applied to the set {1,2,3} sends:
questions.explanation: The cycle (1 2 3) means 1 maps to 2, 2 maps to 3, and 3 maps back to 1.

questions.question: For a finite group G with |G| = p^n·m where p is prime and p does not divide m, a Sylow p-subgroup is:
options: a subgroup of G with order p^n
questions.correct_answer: a subgroup of G with order p^n
questions.explanation: A Sylow p-subgroup is a maximal p-subgroup of G, having order exactly p^n, the full power of p dividing |G|.

questions.question: By Sylow's First Theorem, for any prime p dividing |G|:
options: a Sylow p-subgroup of G always exists
G has no subgroups of order p
questions.correct_answer: a Sylow p-subgroup of G always exists
questions.explanation: Sylow's First Theorem guarantees the existence of at least one Sylow p-subgroup for every prime p dividing the group order.

questions.question: By Sylow's theorems, the number of Sylow p-subgroups of G, denoted np, must satisfy:
options: np ≡ 1 (mod p) and np divides the index [G:P]
questions.correct_answer: np ≡ 1 (mod p) and np divides the index [G:P]
questions.explanation: This is the congruence and divisibility condition from Sylow's Third Theorem constraining the number of Sylow p-subgroups.

questions.question: The external direct product G × H of two groups is defined with componentwise operation, and its order satisfies:
questions.explanation: The direct product's underlying set is the Cartesian product G×H, so its order is the product of the two orders.

questions.question: A ring (R, +, ×) is an algebraic structure in which:
options: (R,+) is an abelian group and × is associative and distributes over +
questions.correct_answer: (R,+) is an abelian group and × is associative and distributes over +
questions.explanation: A ring requires an abelian group under addition, an associative multiplication, and the distributive laws linking the two operations; multiplicative inverses are not required.

questions.question: A subset I of a ring R is called an ideal if:
options: I is an additive subgroup and rI ⊆ I and Ir ⊆ I for all r in R
I contains only the zero element
questions.correct_answer: I is an additive subgroup and rI ⊆ I and Ir ⊆ I for all r in R
questions.explanation: An ideal must absorb multiplication by any ring element from either side, in addition to being closed under addition (analogous to a normal subgroup).

questions.question: An integral domain is a commutative ring with unity that has:
options: a division for every nonzero element
questions.correct_answer: no zero divisors
questions.explanation: An integral domain is a commutative ring with 1 ≠ 0 in which the product of any two nonzero elements is nonzero (no zero divisors).

questions.question: A field is defined as a commutative ring with unity in which:
options: every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse
every element is its own inverse
questions.correct_answer: every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse
questions.explanation: A field extends the integral domain concept by requiring that every nonzero element be invertible under multiplication.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a field?
options: the set of 2×2 matrices under standard operations
questions.correct_answer: the rational numbers Q
questions.explanation: Q is a field because every nonzero rational number has a multiplicative inverse; Z fails since, e.g., 2 has no integer inverse.
